newsitem.title: UK: West cautious on Milosevic concessions.
newsitem.headline: West cautious on Milosevic concessions.

text.p: The West's cautious reaction to concessions by Serbian President Milosevic reflects long and bitter experience of the Balkan quagmire, but also differences among the major powers and wariness about Serbia's opposition.

After a two-month mass protest campaign on the streets, the opposition scored a major victory on Tuesday when electoral officials finally acknowledged they had won municipal elections in the capital Belgrade and Nis, Serbia's second biggest city.
The United States and its European allies have been calling for this and yet the reaction from Western capitals was muted.

Diplomats said the concessions were only partial and could be challenged by by hardliners in the Serbian government. They said it was far from clear that Milosevic had lost the struggle, or that the opposition Zajedno coalition was now going to win.

Underlining the point, a senior hardliner in Milosevic's Socialists said on Wednesday the party would appeal against the electoral ruling and Zajedno vowed to continue protests until its victories in all 14 out of 18 cities were acknowledged.
The United States, so far the only major Western country to comment publicly on the new developments, welcomed the concessions but said it remained sceptical.

"This appears to be a step in the right direction," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "However, the United States will withhold final judgment...until we can see that this result is actually implemented."

European diplomats said Britain and France were still of the view that Milosevic could survive his greatest challenge in nine years of authoritarian rule, although the United States favours a more active strategy to bring democracy to Serbia.

Milosevic cast off communism to become a fervent nationalist in the runup to the war in former Yugoslavia, and then recast himself again as a peacemaker indispensable to the West as it struggled to end the conflict.

The major powers involved in former Yugoslavia -- the United States, Russia, France, Germany and Britain -- have developed a grudging admiration for his survival skills in the murky intricacies of Balkan politics.
"Nobody would want to say that Milosevic is finished at this stage," said one European envoy. "He's under serious pressure, but we may still have to work with him when this is over."

It also remains unclear, diplomats said, whether the opposition coalition could sustain protests or govern effectively in Serbia's cities. The coalition is an uneasy mixture of nationalists and pro-democracy moderates, united in their opposition to Milosevic.
Another key point is that Western powers and Russia do not agree on how best to push Milosevic down the road to democracy.
Diplomats said Russia, which supported Serbia during much of the Yugoslav conflict, had argued against sanctions at a meeting of the five major powers in Brussels last weekend.

Moscow could block any move to reimpose sanctions on Serbia at the United Nations and diplomats say the West would be unwilling to risk a row with Russia at a time of delicate negotiations over NATO's plans for enlargement.
The United States has said it is considering new ways to put pressure on Milosevic, including bannning new trade and high-level contacts with Belgrade.
